lead.headline: Netanyahu offers unity talks 'without preconditions'; Eisenkot calls it 'another spin'
lead.standfirst: A week into Gadi Eisenkot's turn at forming a government, the two largest parties are talking, but they disagree on who could sit in a shared coalition.
paragraphs: On Saturday evening Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Gadi Eisenkot, who holds the mandate to form the next government, to open talks 'without preconditions' on a unity government that would include the Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties. The Times of Israel noted that, unlike in earlier calls, Netanyahu did not say he would lead it. He argued that a government relying on Arab parties could not confront Iran, which he said is working to restore its nuclear program. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich urged Eisenkot to accept.

Eisenkot called the offer 'another spin' and said negotiating teams from his Yashar party and Likud were already due to meet on Sunday. He ruled out a partnership with Netanyahu himself but said he is open to Likud without him, and that Likud must break with 'the extremists'. He named Tuesday's Knesset vote on appointing Matan Kahana as speaker as Likud's next test. The numbers explain the standoff: Likud has 27 seats and Yashar 21, Netanyahu's bloc has 53, Eisenkot's bloc 48 and the Arab parties 19, so nobody reaches the 61 needed alone. Eisenkot has 28 days from receiving the mandate, with a possible 14-day extension.

briefs.headline: Woman killed in Kafr Manda grenade attack; Herzog says she is the year's 200th Arab murder victim
briefs.text: Lina Qassem Zidan, 51, was killed and three people were wounded on Saturday when a grenade was thrown at a shop in the northern town of Kafr Manda, police and medics said. Police arrested three suspects. President Isaac Herzog said she was the 200th murder victim in the Arab community this year and urged the next government to 'intensify the fight' against criminal organizations and illegal weapons. Later that night a 59-year-old man was shot dead in Taibeh in what police called an apparently criminal shooting.

briefs.headline: Hamas sources say Rafah Brigade commander killed in Khan Younis strike
briefs.text: The IDF and Shin Bet said overnight that they had targeted a 'senior terrorist in Hamas's military wing'. Hamas sources told Reuters that Samir Abu Younis, commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed in an airstrike in Khan Younis; Israel has not confirmed that. Earlier on Saturday, Palestinian media reported two people killed in a drone strike in northern Gaza City; the IDF said it targeted two operatives. Separately, the EU demanded 'immediate, unimpeded access' for aid after floods in Gaza, and COGAT, the Israeli defense body that coordinates with Gaza, said it had stepped up sanitation work before the rains.

briefs.headline: Report: Shin Bet questioned Joint List activists about rival party Ra'am
briefs.text: Channel 12 reported that the Shin Bet security service questioned activists from the Joint List and pressed them for information about the rival Islamist party Ra'am; one activist said an investigator tried to recruit him. The Shin Bet said it is acting within its legal authority in a probe into suspected 'subversion and foreign influence' around the election. Central Elections Committee chair Noam Sohlberg said the probe has not yet produced evidence of wrongdoing.

briefs.headline: Israeli delegation flies to Dubai over the flydubai cockpit attack
briefs.text: A Transportation Ministry delegation led by Moshe Ben Zaken is due in Dubai on Sunday to be briefed on the September 30 attack on flydubai Flight FZ1073, in which, according to the report, the copilot attacked the captain with an emergency axe and tried to crash the plane. The ministry will decide afterward whether flydubai can resume flights to Israel.

items.label: US news
items.headline: Trump has told advisers he may hold off on attacking Iran if it does not provoke the US, Reuters reports
paragraphs: President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may not resume strikes on Iran as long as the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or from the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters. The sources said he has made no commitment either way. A White House official said: 'Only President Trump knows what he will do, and when.' Trump has said he will keep the naval blockade and sanctions in place.

According to the report, the Saudi crown prince and Turkey's president both urged Trump not to restart attacks, and US intelligence assesses that the blockade is hurting Iran's economy while new strikes would not much change Iran's negotiating demands. Qatar-mediated talks continue but gaps remain, including over Iran's stock of highly enriched uranium. The pressure runs both ways: Iran's forces said three oil tankers caught fire on Saturday after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
items.why_it_matters: The war that began on February 28 has raised fuel prices and, in a Reuters/Ipsos poll, 55% of Americans said it was not worth the cost. Whether the US strikes again or relies on economic pressure affects oil prices worldwide and directly shapes Israel's own decisions on Iran.

items.label: Stock market
items.headline: Nvidia falls back below $4 trillion after a bank downgrade, while Apple hits a record
paragraphs: Nvidia shares fell about 2% on Friday to $162.85, after a drop of more than 4% on Thursday, the day Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive. That put the company's market value back under $4 trillion. HSBC cut its rating on the stock from 'buy' to 'hold' and lowered its price target from $365 to $170; its analyst, Frank Lee, said 'the uncertainties will prevail' until a permanent successor is named.

Investors moved toward companies seen as safer. Apple, which has largely stayed out of the race to build AI data centers, touched a record $360.80, a market value above $5.2 trillion. The Nasdaq fell 0.91% on Friday and the S&P 500 fell 0.4%, but the S&P still gained 2.5% over the week, its best week since August, CNBC reported. Traders now treat an interest-rate increase at the Federal Reserve's December 9 meeting as a near certainty.
items.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest companies in the major indexes, so doubt about its leadership moves the whole market and anyone holding an index fund. It also shows how much of the AI boom's confidence was tied to one person.

stories.headline: NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google and Meta agree to steer one shared open-source inference engine
stories.standfirst: Fierce rivals in AI chips will sit at the same table to plan SGLang, free software that runs AI models for real users.
stories.what_happened: LMSYS Org, a nonprofit, announced the SGLang Consortium on November 12 at the first SGLang Summit in San Francisco. The eight founding members are NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Cloudflare, Modal and RadixArk. Each names a technical representative and attends two roadmap meetings a year, and members contribute engineering help, testing resources and feedback from their deployments. The project's own maintainers keep the final say over technical decisions and what code gets accepted. LMSYS says SGLang already runs on hundreds of thousands of GPUs, including at Meta, Microsoft, Google and Amazon. The announcement contains no new performance numbers.
stories.what_it_means: Training is how an AI model is built; inference is the model actually answering people. An inference engine is the program that sits between the model and the chips: it loads the model, lines up many users' requests, groups them so the GPU stays busy, and remembers earlier work so it is not redone. SGLang is one such engine, and it is open source, meaning anyone can use and change it for free. The consortium is like competing car makers agreeing to jointly maintain the same road: each still sells its own cars (chips), but all of them benefit if the road is smooth.
stories.why_it_matters: LMSYS cites a Deloitte projection that inference will be about two-thirds of all AI computing this year, so small software gains save enormous amounts of hardware and electricity. For NVIDIA, good open software makes its chips more useful; for AMD and Intel, a shared engine means their chips are supported from day one. In practice: a company serving its own chatbot with SGLang can expect it to work well on whichever maker's chips it buys.
terms: Inference
Running a trained AI model to produce answers, as opposed to training it.
Inference engine
The software that loads a model onto chips and serves many users' requests efficiently.
Open source
Software whose code is public, so anyone can use, inspect and improve it.
Consortium
A group of organizations that agree to work together on a shared project.

stories.headline: OpenAI gives its agents a wallet that can pay without ever seeing your card number
stories.standfirst: ChatGPT Wallet lets an AI agent finish a purchase on a store's website, with your approval for each one.
stories.what_happened: OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on November 13, built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa. It works through 'dots', OpenAI's personal agents. When the agent is ready to buy something, the user approves that purchase with a check such as Face ID or a fingerprint. The card network then issues a stand-in card number, security code and expiry date for the merchant, so neither the agent nor the store receives the real card details. For now it is limited to US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and over with eligible US cards. OpenAI says future versions could add spending caps and category limits, and warns that some stores' fraud systems may wrongly block these purchases.
stories.what_it_means: An AI agent is a model that does not just answer but takes actions, like filling in a checkout page. The obvious danger is handing software your credit card. The fix here is called tokenization: instead of the real number, the network creates a substitute number that stands in for it. It is like giving a valet a key that only starts the car and cannot open the glovebox: useful for the one job, useless if stolen. Each purchase still needs your approval, so the agent is not yet shopping on its own.
stories.why_it_matters: Paying is the last step that kept agents from completing real errands. A concrete use: ask the agent to find a specific phone charger under a price, it fills the cart on the store's site, you approve with your face, and it is ordered. Open questions remain: reports note OpenAI has not said who bears the cost when an agent buys the wrong thing.
terms: AI agent
An AI model that takes actions step by step, such as clicking and filling in forms, instead of only replying with text.
Tokenization (payments)
Replacing a real card number with a substitute number so the real one is never shared.
Biometric check
Proving it's you with your face or fingerprint.

stories.headline: OpenAI breaks up its stand-alone robotics team, Fortune reports
stories.standfirst: The robotics staff were moved into the company's main research and product groups; OpenAI says robots are still part of its plan.
stories.what_happened: Fortune reported on November 13 that OpenAI has dissolved its separate robotics team, according to coverage citing the article. Research staff moved into the main research group under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, and applied robotics and hardware staff moved into the Applied organization under President Greg Brockman. An OpenAI spokesperson said robotics 'remains a core part of OpenAI's long-term vision'. Fortune did not report how many people were on the team or whether anyone left. The stand-alone team was formed in 2024; OpenAI had closed an earlier robotics team in 2020.
stories.what_it_means: A company can build robot intelligence in two ways: a dedicated group that builds a special model just for robots, or the same general model that powers its chatbot, taught to also control a body. Folding the robotics people into the main teams points toward the second approach, though OpenAI has not said so explicitly. Think of it as closing the separate 'robot department' and seating those engineers with everyone else.
stories.why_it_matters: It is a signal about where the field may be heading: one general model for text, images and physical action, rather than a separate brain per job. If that works, improvements to the main model would flow to robots automatically. It is a reorganization, not a product, so nothing changes for users today.
terms: General model
One AI model meant to handle many kinds of tasks, rather than one built for a single job.

nature.headline: This little brown mushroom is laced with a hallucinogen and lethal toxins
nature.standfirst: A Florida fungus is the first known to make both the 'magic mushroom' drug and the poison found in death caps.
paragraphs: Mushrooms that make psilocybin, the mind-altering chemical in 'magic mushrooms', and mushrooms that make amatoxins, the poisons behind most deadly mushroom poisonings, were thought to be separate groups. Researchers at the University of Florida have now found one species that makes both. It is called Galerina indica, and the team nicknamed it the 'dark magic mushroom'.

Andrew Kunik, then an undergraduate, found it while cataloguing fungi at a university research station, where it grows on rotting palm trunks. Two kinds of evidence were matched: the mushroom's genome (its full set of genetic instructions) and a chemical analysis of what is actually inside it. Both pointed to the same answer. Nobody yet knows why it makes both; Nature's summary says the mix may deter hungry animals. The full Nature article is behind a login, so this summary relies on Nature's short description, the university's report and the study in Current Biology.
key_points: What they found: one mushroom species, Galerina indica, produces both psilocybin and deadly amatoxins, a combination not seen before.
How: they read the mushroom's genome and separately tested its chemistry, and the two results agreed.

Why it matters: it gives scientists a natural test case for why fungi make these chemicals at all, and it is a warning for foragers, because it looks like hundreds of other small brown mushrooms and turns blue when handled, as some psychedelic ones do.
terms: Psilocybin
The chemical in 'magic mushrooms' that causes hallucinations.
Amatoxins
A family of mushroom poisons that destroy the liver; they are what makes the death cap deadly.
Genome
The complete set of genetic instructions of a living thing.

lead.headline: SpaceX catches a Starship returning from orbit for the first time; the booster is lost
lead.standfirst: The launch tower's arms caught the upper stage after about a day in space, the step that makes reusing the whole rocket possible.
paragraphs: Late Saturday night Israel time, shortly before 11:30 pm, the Starship upper stage of Flight 15 came back from orbit and was caught in mid-air by the mechanical arms of the launch tower at Starbase, Texas. It had launched on Friday, spent roughly 22 hours in orbit and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites. It is the first time a ship of this kind has been recovered this way. SpaceX wrote: 'Mechazilla catches Starship!'

The plan was to catch both halves of the rocket. That did not happen: the Super Heavy booster, the lower stage, had a problem on its way back, called off its catch and steered to the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded before reaching the water, Engadget reported. Why the catch matters: until now the upper stage was thrown away or ditched in the ocean on every flight. Catching it on the tower, with no landing legs, is how SpaceX intends to refuel and refly the same vehicle quickly. It has still not recovered both stages on one flight, or reflown a recovered ship.

study.track: Sunday track: XLIO and kernel bypass
study.title: What a network card does: packet rings, descriptors and DMA
study.big_idea: A network card and the software that drives it talk through a shared to-do list in memory: the software lists empty buffers, the card fills them with arriving packets by writing straight into memory, and marks each one done. No one hands packets over one by one.
background: A network card (NIC) turns electrical or optical signals on the cable into bytes, and back. But the card is a separate device from the CPU and its memory. So there has to be an agreed way for the card to say 'here is a packet' and for the software to say 'send this'. The software that speaks the card's language is called the driver; in normal Linux it lives in the kernel, and with XLIO part of that job moves into your own program.

The first building block is DMA, direct memory access. It means the card itself can read and write the computer's main memory (RAM) over the PCIe bus, without the CPU copying each byte. The CPU only tells the card which memory addresses to use. Those addresses must stay valid, so the memory is pinned: the operating system promises not to move it or swap it out.

The second building block is the ring. A ring is a fixed-size array used in a circle: when you reach the last slot you continue at the first. Each slot holds a descriptor, a tiny record (typically 16 to 64 bytes) that says 'the buffer is at this address and is this long'. A descriptor is like a parking ticket: it is not the car, it says where the car is.
steps: Setup: the driver allocates packet buffers (for example 2 KB each, enough for a normal 1,500-byte packet), pins them, and creates a receive ring and a transmit ring, commonly 1,024 slots each.

Stocking the receive ring: the driver writes one descriptor per empty buffer into the receive ring, then tells the card 'slots up to here are ready' by writing a number to a card register. That write is nicknamed ringing the doorbell.

A packet arrives: the card takes the next descriptor, writes the packet's bytes straight into that buffer by DMA, and records the result (length, checksum OK or not) in a completion entry. On ConnectX cards these completions go to a separate ring called the completion queue.
Noticing: the software learns about it either because the card raises an interrupt, or because the software keeps checking the completion ring itself, which is called polling.

Processing and refilling: the software reads the completion, hands the buffer up to the TCP/IP code, and puts a fresh empty buffer's descriptor back into the ring. If it does not refill fast enough, the ring runs empty and the card drops packets.

Sending is the mirror image: the software writes a descriptor pointing at the data to send into the transmit ring and rings the doorbell; the card reads the data by DMA, puts it on the wire, and posts a completion so the buffer can be reused.
study.example: Run 'ethtool -g eth0' on a Linux server and you see the ring sizes, often RX 1024 and TX 1024. Now picture a burst of 5,000 packets arriving while the CPU core is busy for a moment. The ring has only 1,024 stocked buffers. Once those are full, the card has nowhere to write and drops the rest; 'ethtool -S' shows the count in a counter with a name like rx_out_of_buffer. Making the ring bigger (ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096) absorbs bigger bursts, at the cost of more memory and buffers that are less likely to be in the CPU's cache.
study.why_xlio: Kernel bypass is, at its core, giving a user-space program its own rings. XLIO asks the ConnectX card for private receive, send and completion queues, registers its own buffers (in hugepages) for DMA, and has the card steer the application's connections into those rings. Then XLIO polls the completion queue directly from your process: packets go card to application memory with no kernel in between. The ring sizes are tunable (XLIO_RX_WRE and XLIO_TX_WRE).
numbers: Smallest-packet rate on a 10 Gb/s link
about 14.88 million packets per second, one every 67 nanoseconds
Smallest-packet rate on a 100 Gb/s link
study.pitfall: Misconception: the ring holds the packets. It does not. The ring holds small descriptors that point to buffers elsewhere in memory. That is why a ring of 1,024 entries is tiny in itself, and why the real memory cost is the buffers behind it. A related mistake: thinking a bigger ring is always better. It hides bursts but adds memory, hurts cache behaviour, and can let packets sit longer before anyone looks at them.
terms: NIC
Network interface card: the hardware that sends and receives packets.
Driver
The software that knows how to talk to one specific device.
DMA
Direct memory access: the device reads or writes main memory itself, without the CPU copying each byte.
Pinned memory
Memory the operating system promises not to move or swap out, so a device can safely use its address.
Descriptor
A small record in a ring that says where a buffer is and how big it is.
Ring
A fixed-size array used in a circle, shared between the software and the card.
Doorbell
A write to a card register that tells the card 'there is new work in the ring'.
Completion queue
A ring where the card reports each finished receive or send.
study.question: A server shows a growing 'out of buffer' drop counter on its network card, yet the CPU is only 30% busy on average. How can packets be dropped when the CPU has spare time?
study.answer: Drops depend on moments, not averages. The receive ring only holds a fixed number of empty buffers, about 1,024 by default. If packets arrive in a burst faster than the software refills the ring, even for a millisecond, the card runs out of places to write and drops packets. At 10 Gb/s a small packet can arrive every 67 nanoseconds, so 1,024 slots can fill in well under a millisecond. Fixes: refill faster (polling, a dedicated core), spread traffic over more rings, or enlarge the ring.
